title: Nehemiah 10:28–39
context: The rest of the people join their leaders in a curse and an oath to walk in God’s law. They pledge to avoid intermarriage with the peoples of the land, to keep the Sabbath and the seventh year, and to support the temple through a yearly charge, the wood offering, first fruits, firstborn, and tithes, ending with the resolve, “We will not forsake the house of our God.”

verses.text: The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all those who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters—everyone who had knowledge and understanding—
verses.arminianNotes: “The rest of the people,” including families and “everyone who had knowledge and understanding,” join in. Arminian readers see the whole community freely entering the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see broad participation in the renewal. The mention of those who had separated themselves “to the law of God” shows that commitment to God’s law defined membership in the community.

verses.text: joined with their brothers, their nobles, and entered into a curse and into an oath, to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his ordinances and his statutes;
verses.arminianNotes: They enter “into a curse and into an oath, to walk in God’s law.” Arminian readers see a serious, freely made pledge to obey God, with real accountability attached.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant renewal expressed through an oath. Both traditions read the verse as a serious pledge of obedience under God’s law, freely taken by the whole community.

verses.text: and that we would not give our daughters to the peoples of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons;
verses.arminianNotes: They pledge “that we would not give our daughters to the peoples of the land.” Arminian readers see commitment to covenant faithfulness in family life, recalling Deuteronomy 7:3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the concern to guard against idolatry through marriage. Nehemiah 13:23–27 shows this pledge later broken, which the later chapter records without resolving it here.

verses.text: and if the peoples of the land bring wares or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy from them on the Sabbath, or on a holy day; and that we would forego the seventh year crops and the exaction of every debt.
verses.arminianNotes: They pledge not to buy on the Sabbath and to forego seventh-year crops and debts. Arminian readers see obedience reaching into commerce and economic life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the law shaping daily practice. Exodus 23:10–11 and Deuteronomy 15:1–2 lie behind these pledges, and Nehemiah 13:15–22 later records Sabbath violations.

verses.text: Also we made ordinances for ourselves, to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God:
verses.arminianNotes: They charge themselves “yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God.” Arminian readers see willing support for God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the community providing for worship. Exodus 30:13 speaks of a half shekel, and interpreters differ on how this third of a shekel relates to it.

verses.text: for the show bread, for the continual meal offering, for the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, for the new moons, for the set feasts, for the holy things, for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The money supports the show bread, offerings, Sabbaths, feasts, sin offerings, and “all the work of the house of our God.” Arminian readers see worship sustained through shared responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ordered worship of the temple maintained. The mention of sin offerings “to make atonement for Israel” keeps the need for atonement central to the community’s life.

verses.text: We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers’ houses, at times appointed year by year, to burn on the LORD our God’s altar, as it is written in the law;
verses.arminianNotes: They cast lots for the wood offering “to burn on the LORD our God’s altar, as it is written in the law.” Arminian readers see practical arrangements made to keep worship continuous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lot used to share responsibilities fairly. The specific wood offering is not detailed in the Torah, and readers often connect it with the command to keep the altar fire burning in Leviticus 6:12–13.

verses.text: and to bring the first fruits of our ground and the first fruits of all fruit of all kinds of trees, year by year, to the LORD’s house;
verses.arminianNotes: They pledge to bring “the first fruits of our ground and the first fruits of all fruit of all kinds of trees.” Arminian readers see gratitude expressed by offering the first of the harvest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see first fruits acknowledging God as the giver of the land’s produce. The pledge reflects commands such as Exodus 23:19 and Deuteronomy 26:1–11.

verses.text: also the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks, to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God;
verses.arminianNotes: They pledge to bring “the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the law.” Arminian readers see devotion acknowledging God’s claim on the firstborn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see obedience to laws such as Exodus 13:2, 13, where firstborn sons are redeemed. The pledge recognizes that all life belongs to God.

verses.text: and that we should bring the first fruits of our dough, our wave offerings, the fruit of all kinds of trees, and the new wine and the oil, to the priests, to the rooms of the house of our God; and the tithes of our ground to the Levites; for they, the Levites, take the tithes in all our farming villages.
verses.arminianNotes: They pledge first fruits of dough, offerings, new wine, oil, and tithes to the Levites. Arminian readers see generous support for those who serve in God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see provision for the Levites according to the law. Numbers 15:20 and Numbers 18:21 lie behind these pledges, and Nehemiah 13:10–14 later records neglect of the Levites’ portions.

verses.text: The priest, the descendent of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites take tithes. The Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the rooms, into the treasure house.
verses.arminianNotes: A priest accompanies the Levites when they collect tithes, and the Levites bring “the tithe of the tithes” to the treasure house. Arminian readers see accountability in handling sacred gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see orderly stewardship of offerings. The tithe of the tithes reflects Numbers 18:26, ensuring that the Levites also gave from what they received.

verses.text: For the children of Israel and the children of Levi shall bring the wave offering of the grain, of the new wine, and of the oil, to the rooms where the vessels of the sanctuary are, and the priests who minister, with the gatekeepers and the singers. We will not forsake the house of our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The offerings go to the rooms of the sanctuary, and the people declare, “We will not forsake the house of our God.” Arminian readers see a heartfelt commitment to sustain worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the climax of the pledge. The resolution not to forsake God’s house is shared ground about renewed obedience, even though Nehemiah 13 shows how quickly commitments can falter.
